'''Dubie:''' {{legend0|#FFB2B2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#D75D5D|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Jim Douglas]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Peter Shumlin]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsVT}} The '''2010 Vermont gubernatorial general election''' took place on November 2.{{cite web |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Vermont_gubernatorial_election,_2010 |title=Vermont Gubernatorial Election, 2010 |website=Ballotpedia |publisher=Lucy Burns Institute |location=Middleton, WI |access-date=January 19, 2021 |quote=}} Vermont and [[New Hampshire]] are the only two states where the governor serves a two-year term instead of four.{{cite news |last=Allen |first=Anne Wallace |date=February 3, 2019 |title=Vermont governors are divided on question of 4-year terms |url=https://vtdigger.org/2019/02/03/vermont-governors-divided-question-4-year-terms/ |work=VT Digger |location=MOntpelier, VT}} Primary elections took place on August 24. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Jim Douglas]] was not a candidate for re-election.{{cite news |date=August 27, 2009 |title=Vermont Governor Douglas will not seek re-election |url=https://vermontbiz.com/news/2009/august/27/vermont-governor-douglas-will-not-seek-re-election |work=Vermont Biz.com |publisher=Vermont Business Magazine |location=South Burlington, VT}} [[Brian Dubie]], the incumbent [[Lieutenant Governor of Vermont|lieutenant governor]], was the Republican nominee. The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nomination was won by [[Peter Shumlin]], the [[President pro tempore of the Vermont Senate]]. The result was a 119,543 (49.5 percent) to 115,212 (47.7 percent) plurality for Shumlin. Several minor candidates got between 600 and 2,000 votes each. In accordance with the Vermont Constitution, if no candidate receives a majority, the contest is decided by the [[Vermont General Assembly]].{{cite news |last=Dobbs |first=Taylor |date=November 6, 2014 |title=Wait, The Legislature Is Choosing The Governor? |url=https://www.vpr.org/post/wait-legislature-choosing-governor |work=Vermont Public Radio |location=Colchester, VT}} In such races, the combined Vermont House and Senate almost always chooses the candidate who won a plurality. Dubie indicated on November 3 that he did not intend to ask for a recount or contest the election in the legislature, and conceded to Shumlin.{{cite news |last=Galloway |first=Anne |date=November 3, 2010 |title=Dubie concedes; Shumlin holds victory presser at noon |url=https://vtdigger.org/2010/11/03/dubie-concedes/ |work=VT Digger |location=Montpelier, VT}} On January 6, 2011, with 173 of 180 members voting, 87 votes were necessary for a choice.{{cite news |last=Remsen |first=Nancy |date=January 7, 2011 |title='Regular Guy' Phil Scott sworn in as lt. governor |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/68012017/regular-guy/ |work=[[The Burlington Free Press]] |location=Burlington, VT |page=4 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} The General Assembly elected Shumlin on the first ballot, 145–28. ==Republican primary== ===Candidate=== * [[Brian Dubie]], [[Lieutenant Governor of Vermont|lieutenant governor]]{{cite web |url=http://www.vpr.net/news_detail/85987/ |title=Dubie will run for governor |date=1 October 2009 |first=Ross |last=Sneyd |publisher=[[Vermont Public Radio]]}} ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== * [[Susan Bartlett]], state senator {{cite news|title=Sen.
